(Tuesday through next Sunday)
Issued at 124 PM CDT Sun Oct 25 2026

Midweek moisture will be more plentiful as southerly flow responds 
to broad diffluence over the Rockies and Plains. While there isn't a 
distinct disturbance to take advantage of this moisture Tuesday and 
Wednesday, the moist onshore flow and neutrally stable environment 
afforded by the broad longwave troughing over the western US suggest 
opportunities for scattered light to moderate showers and a few 
isolated thunderstorms Tuesday and Wednesday emanating from the 
coastal bend. Low to medium chances for rain extend from the Coastal 
Plains through the I-35 corridor towards the Hill Country, with the 
best chances (40-50%) south of the San Antonio area Tuesday 
afternoon, shifting eastward to the Highway 77 corridor on Wednesday 
as weak shortwave ridging moves over the area. Regional rain amounts 
should generally be in the range of a few tenths from this activity, 
though an isolated spot could forseeably pick up an inch from a 
heavier shower or storm.

Better rain chances arrive later in the week as a broad trough 
arriving over the Baja California on Thursday results in more 
meridional flow in the subtropical jet. This pattern is well timed 
to siphon off additional moisture and energy from Hurricane Vance, 
which is forecast to decay off the Pacific Mexican coast later this 
week. Modeled PWATs from the long range ensembles are clustered 
around 1.6 to 1.9 inches, or above the 90th percentile for late 
October. This moisture will provide an opportunity for scattered to 
widespread rain with some directly associated with the moisture 
plume and diffluence aloft and others moving inland as feeder 
showers and storms from the coast. The latest models have shown a 
focus for rainfall (both in likelihood and magnitude) mainly 
stretching from the Rio Grande Plains northward to the southern 
Edwards Plateau, aligned with the strongest vapor transport and 
potentially limited on its eastern extent by somewhat more stable 
conditions accompanying the surface high pressure over the Eastern 
US. Rain chances increase Thursday as the moisture arrives, and 
there is good consensus that the rain intensity peaks Thursday night 
through Friday morning as a 30 kt low-level jet ramps up along the 
Rio Grande, likely becoming slightly more diffuse and shifting north 
and east Friday afternoon. The peak rain chances are highest (65-
85%) along the Rio Grande and southern Edwards Plateau, including 
the Del Rio area, and decrease eastward (to about 20-40%) towards 
the Coastal Plains. There has been a recent uptick in mean ensemble 
forecast rain amounts along the Rio Grande and southern Edwards 
Plateau in recent runs, consistent with the focusing of moisture 
over those areas. While the 15-25 kt deep-layer flow should keep 
individual showers moving at a steady clip, the long channel of 
moisture and high PWAT values indicate opportunities for recurring 
and at times heavy rain. The latest ECMWF EFI guidance suggests a 
potential for locally heavier amounts over the southern Edwards 
Plateau and along the Rio Grande. Thus, we'll be keeping an eye on 
a potential isolated flood risk mainly late Thursday into Friday 
morning. At present, the main risk area is west of the I-35 
corridor, extending to the Rio Grande.

The bulk of the tropical Pacific moisture plume should cycle past 
our area by Saturday. A weak shortwave trough may reinvigorate 
showers north of I-10 on Saturday for a final round of wet weather, 
but rain chances generally decrease through the weekend. Skies clear 
some as the shortwave pattern becomes slightly anticyclonic, but the 
continued presence of southwesterly flow aloft will probably keep 
cirrus streaming over the area.

Daytime high temperatures throughout the week are expected to hover 
in the mid 70s to mid 80s, varying with cloud cover and rain. 
Thursday and Friday could trend cooler over the southern Edwards 
Plateau and Rio Grande if the rain signal continues to be 
concentrated there. Overnight temperatures remain steadily in the 
60s, slightly above seasonal normals.
